messages.subject: A strange error with read_cross2
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to read in my data and I am running in to an error:
In align_geno_sex_cross(output$geno, output$is_female, output$cross_info) :
  Omitting genotypes for 1 individual with no sex/cross info

I have re-checked all my files, re-read through the input file documentations, and I cannot figure out why I am getting this error. all of my sample IDs are matched in every single file, they are all in the same order for each file, and they all have full genotype information, sex information, and are included in the cross information. It is the first file that is omitted in the qtl2 object that ends up being generated, and if I remove that first sample then the new first sample throws the same error. So read_cross2() is always having issue with the first sample for some reason.

Any help would be appreciated.

Thank you,
Tyler

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Re: Advanced intercross followed by backcrossing
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl2-disc] Re: Advanced intercross followed by backcrossing
messages.body_plain:
I wouldn't analyze just 1 MB at a time; rather I would omit redundant markers, or otherwise try to bin/merge the polymorphisms.

Can you give me a sense of the scale of the problem? How many SNPs and how many individuals?

karl

On Tue, Sep 8, 2026 at 9:14 AM Tyler Audet <tjm....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm not sure if I should start another thread or not, but I have gotten to the point in the explained above project where I actually have my sequencing and am trying to start getting qtl2 to work. Right now I'm having memory issues just making the qtl2 object, and it is because I am using SNPs, or 75bp fragments as my markers, and the shear number of SNPs in the genome that I have is not feasible for r and I'm running in to memory issues. Surely I'm not the first person to use whole genomes, and I've seen that there is a genome scan function, but I can't even load one chromosome worth of data in to r as the qtl2 cross object. Is it typical to break your genome up in to like 1Mb fragments to reduce memory usage? I worry that would break up recombination blocks and things wouldn't be getting analyzed properly? Is there a simpler way to deal with memory issues?
>
> Sorry if this is a stupid question,
> Tyler
>

> On Monday, 11 May 2026 at 15:40:12 UTC+2 Karl Broman wrote:
> > Treating it as an AIL should be okay.
> >
> > Alternatively, use "genail2" so that you can account for genotypes not being 50:50 between the two parents.
> > See my 2022 paper on "A generic HMM for multi-parent populations", https://doi.org/10.1093/g3journal/jkab396
> >
> > karl
> >
> > On Monday, May 11, 2026 at 8:10:18 AM UTC-5 tjm....@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hello, I have an experiment that I am beginning to prepare for sequencing and analysis to map loci associated with a trait in one species by hybridising it with a sister species (that lacks the trait) for 5 generations. So I have an F5 advanced intercross, however, to narrow down out haplotype blocks, the F5 hybrids were mated back to the sister species and allowed to go to a new F2. So I have and F5 advanced intercross, stacked on to an F2 backcross.
> > >
> > > My current thought would be to treat it as an F7 AIL, but this seems like it may violate the assumptions of the AIL because at F5 everything is re-combining with the parental sister species genome again.
> > >
> > > Do you think I could just treat it as an AIL, or is there another way to set this up better?
> > >
> > > Thank you for any help.
>
